Here's the problem. You need storage and a delivery system too. Solar power harnessing is expensive in those small lots (in comparison to a solar farm). I run solar (that I installed) at my house and on my camper van. To power basic appliances in the van with low amp/volts it takes FOUR 3ft by 2 ft (roughly) to run the appliances in my camper for 8 hours straight on a full charge. That's: a small TV, a microwave for no more than 5 minutes, a very efficient small refrigerator, LED lights (SUPER low amps), and a small portable AC for up to two hours. To do this it needs 60% of good sun coverage a day. When they get dirty you lose efficiency, when birds shit on them, they get scratched etc. Solar is cool, but it's more of a supplementary thing unless you live your life AROUND the solar. You can run your house on full solar but it takes about 18 panels (65in by 39in) for a 2k sqft home with low electricity usage. I buy everything I can from GOG and only use Steam when there's no other option. Why? DRM, plain and simple. A game without DRM will always be superior to the same game with DRM.

GOG.com all the way (plus some much smaller direct sales).

It provides installers so that you can install it on any computer that lacks internet access. Very handy to have an offline copy of your library for when your ISP fucks up, your ISP cuts you off, you get banned from the service, or the service shuts down. This is probably a struggle for people who own every single game. I have a mere 197 separate games (some get bought as a single item though) and I am up to 282 GiB of space require for them all and nearly every single "added extra". It is my impression that all games which require them, the installers come bundled with and run the redistributables that they need. That is DirectX versions, C runtime libraries, .NET, whatever other shit.

People will claim that you can do most of this with Steam as well. Yes not all games require its client to be running or even installed. I don't believe you can discover this through first-party sources. This means you can copy around those games as you want. This has all the problems of a manual backup. It will not include start menu shortcuts, redistributables.

The Galaxy client is almost completely optional. They claim it is completely optional. I call this a lie because it is required for some online features of a few games, usually multiplayer. I don't use it and only had it installed once so I can't say what it is like. I reckon it is like most other browsers masquerading as another program: bloated and slow.

Now my opinion of Steam is completely jaded by the one and only game I have that needs it. Civilization 5. I was unaware that I was not buying a game on disc, despite the pressed DVD in the box, but really a Steam key that I could use on their service. I was required to install the Steam client. I was required to create an account. I had difficultly installing it at the time because their servers were overloaded. Hardly surprising since it was a brand new release.

I am now extremely vigilant when looking at games that are not on GOG.com. I look out for the Steam logo. I look out for the word steam. I treat either of these to mean I would be buying a Steam key through a Steam front unless otherwise is explicitly mentioned.

Now this is where Steam's DRM comes into it all. I am aware that not all games have it or that not all games are integrated with Steamworks. (Are they the same thing? I've never seen anyone be explicitly clear about it link to any document that is.) These make it very hard to play a game offline. I recall that the last time I tried to play I could not because I had not left the client in offline mode and you need to login first before you can put it into offline mode.

Sure this all sound like a problem you think you'll never have but get burned one time and you'll carry the same grudge as I do.

Now I have an even bigger problem with the Steam Workshop, especially how they appear to want to gain a monopoly over modding but that requires an even longer discussion which involves the rest of modern software and its distribution.. I will sum it up as that it seems extremely dangerous and will lead an Apple-style walled garden where everything must have their approval and no slightly controversial content is tolerated.

I use both, but GOG usually gets my lunch money, especially during the seasonal sales. The games (or at least the Linux WINE wrapped ones) generally work better than what's on Steam. Plus, GOG just has more of what I want to play.

Pretty much everyone has commented on the DRM situation, and I agree that DRM-free is always preferable (although Steamworks is vastly preferable to most pre-Steam DRM schemes, notable always-online and activation limits). Steam also tends to have better sales and prices in general, with GOG only really having a summer and winter sale.

The reason I like GOG is the extreme lengths they go to to get older games working seamlessly as possible. Fallout, Roller Coaster Tycoon 1+2, Rayman, and Rayman 2 all work very well, even on my modern system, despite being so old that they have no right to run easily. I've never had any trouble with any game from GOG. They even have a refund policy specifically to cover edge cases where a game wouldn't work, and it is still looser than Steam's refund policy. My only real problem was the fact that I tended to overlook GOG games when looking for something to play because they didn't have a client, but Galaxy has worked fine for me and helps manage them quite nicely.

All in all, it comes off as GOG's team actually caring about the games that they sell and trying to make it so people can still play older games easily. Pretty much every game on GOG would be easily pirated (in fact a lot of torrents just distribute GOG's installer, most recently NMS), but the work put in is worth buying from them, at least to me.
If I can get it on GoG, I will. DRM is the main reason. I don't see it happening any time soon, but should Steam go down, I don't want all that money from games gone with them.
